title: An ant on a stretching rope.
blocks: An ant starts walking along a rubber rope one kilometer long, at one centimeter per second. At the same time, the rope starts stretching by one kilometer every second. Can the ant ever reach the end?
Here are the rules. The rope stretches evenly, so the ant is carried forward as it stretches. Its own speed never changes. Does it get there?
It looks impossible. The ant moves one centimeter per second, and the end of the rope runs away a hundred thousand times faster than that.

But the ant does reach the end. The trick is to track the fraction of the rope it has covered. After the first second, it has covered one hundred-thousandth of the rope. After the second, the rope is longer, so the same step covers a smaller fraction, but the ant keeps all its earlier progress.

After a thousand seconds, it has covered about seven thousandths of a percent. After a billion seconds, about two hundredths of a percent. The fractions add up as one plus one half plus one third, and so on, the harmonic series, which never stops growing.

So the ant arrives, after about e to the power of one hundred thousand seconds. That's a number with over forty-three thousand digits. Infinite doesn't mean never, and slow doesn't mean stuck. Even the slowest growth wins, if it never stops.
